title: Portuguese Empire
capsule: The Portuguese Empire, the first and longest-lived of the European overseas empires, grew from Prince Henry the Navigator's early 15th-century Atlantic expeditions into a seaborne trading network spanning West Africa, Brazil, India, Southeast Asia, and East Africa. Vasco da Gama's 1498 voyage to Calicut opened the Indian Ocean spice trade, and by the 1510s Afonso de Albuquerque had seized Goa, Malacca, and Hormuz as strategic chokepoints. The union of the Iberian crowns under Philip II of Spain (1580–1640) led to Dutch and English attacks that stripped the empire of most of its Asian trade posts; Brazil, the empire's most valuable possession, declared independence in 1822. The attested span ends in 1823, reflecting the loss of Brazil; Portugal retained African colonies until 1975.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Coastal trading-post territories are well documented through the Casa da India's administrative records and cartography; inland territorial claims in Africa and Brazil were largely notional before the 19th century; moderate confidence for Brazil's colonial interior, high confidence for coastal enclaves.
